description: C++ specific semantic errors (streams, classes, overloading, conversions).

rules.title: << and >> mixed up with cin / cout
rules.what: The stream on line {line} is used with the wrong arrow. `cout` (output) uses `<<`, `cin` (input) uses `>>`.
why: Think of the arrows as the direction the data flows: `cout << x` sends x OUT to the screen, `cin >> x` brings input IN to x.
fix: Use `cin >> x;` for input and `cout << x;` for output.
rules.tip: C++ printed a very long list of 'candidates' for this mistake. You can ignore all of them - they are just every version of << the library contains.
samples: no match for 'operator<<' (operand types are 'std::istream' {aka 'std::basic_istream<char>'} and 'int')
invalid operands to binary expression ('istream' (aka 'basic_istream<char>') and 'int')

rules.title: No version of the function accepts these arguments
rules.what: The call `{call}` on line {line} does not match any version of the function: the number or the types of the arguments are wrong.
why: An argument has the wrong type (e.g. a string where an int is expected).
Too many or too few arguments.
fix: Compare the call with the function's parameter list and pass matching values.
rules.tip: The 'candidate' notes below the error list every version the compiler tried and why it did not fit.
samples: no matching function for call to 'square(const char [2])'
no matching function for call to 'square'

rules.title: Value cannot be converted to the needed type
patterns: ^cannot initialize a (?:variable|parameter|return object) of type '(?P<to>.+?)' with an (?:l|r)value of type '(?P<from>.+?)'$
^ISO C\+\+ forbids comparison between pointer and integer$
rules.what: On line {line} a `{from}` is used where a `{to}` is needed, and C++ will not convert it automatically.
why: Double quotes (a string) used where a single character or number was expected.
A number assigned to a pointer, or a pointer to a number.
fix: Give a value of type `{to}` (convert explicitly if really needed).
samples: invalid conversion from 'int' to 'int*'
conversion from 'int' to non-scalar type 'std::string' {aka 'std::__cxx11::basic_string<char>'} requested
cannot initialize a variable of type 'int *' with an lvalue of type 'int'

rules.title: Accessing a private member of a class
rules.what: `{member}` is a {access} member of class `{cls}`, so code outside the class (like main) cannot use it directly.
why: In a `class`, members are private by default until you write `public:`.
fix: Write `public:` above the members that must be used from outside, or add public getter/setter functions.
samples: 'int Account::balance' is private within this context
'balance' is a private member of 'Account'

rules.title: Narrowing conversion in { } initialisation
patterns: ^type '(?P<from>[^']+)' cannot be narrowed to '(?P<to>[^']+)' in initializer list$
^constant expression evaluates to .* which cannot be narrowed to type '(?P<to>[^']+)'$
^non-constant-expression cannot be narrowed from type '(?P<from>[^']+)' to '(?P<to>[^']+)' in initializer list$
rules.what: Brace initialisation `{ }` does not allow a value to lose information. A `{from}` cannot be squeezed into a `{to}` (the decimals would be cut off).
fix: Use the matching type (`double x{3.7};`) or convert explicitly: `int x{static_cast<int>(3.7)};`.
samples: narrowing conversion of '3.7000000000000002e+0' from 'double' to 'int' [-Wnarrowing]
type 'double' cannot be narrowed to 'int' in initializer list

rules.title: Name clashes with the std library
rules.what: `{name}` could mean two different things here - usually YOUR variable and the standard-library `std::{name}`, because of `using namespace std;`.
why: Global variables named `count`, `max`, `min`, `distance`, `data`, `size`, `next` clash with std functions of the same name.
fix: Rename your variable (e.g. `cnt`, `maxValue`), or remove `using namespace std;` and write `std::` where needed.
samples: reference to 'count' is ambiguous

rules.title: String literal stored in a char* (C++)
patterns: ^ISO C\+\+ forbids converting a string constant to '(?P<to>[^']+)'$
^ISO C\+\+11 does not allow conversion from string literal to '(?P<to>[^']+)'$
^conversion from string literal to '(?P<to>[^']+)' is deprecated$
rules.what: A string literal like `"hello"` is read-only, so in C++ it must be stored in a `const char*` (or a `std::string`), not a plain `char*`.
why: Code written for C (or old C++) that uses `char *s = "...";`.
samples: ISO C++ forbids converting a string constant to 'char*'
ISO C++11 does not allow conversion from string literal to 'char *'

rules.title: Member function used without ()
patterns: ^reference to non-static member function must be called(?:; did you mean to call it with no arguments\?)?$
rules.what: `{member}` is a FUNCTION of the object, so it must be called with brackets: `{member}()`.
fix: Add `()` after the member function name.
samples: reference to non-static member function must be called; did you mean to call it with no arguments?
invalid use of non-static member function 'int A::get()'

rules.title: Literal passed to a reference parameter
patterns: ^cannot bind non-const lvalue reference of type '(?P<to>[^']+)' to an rvalue of type '(?P<from>[^']+)'$
^non-const lvalue reference to type '(?P<to>[^']+)' cannot bind to a temporary of type '(?P<from>[^']+)'$
^invalid initialization of non-const reference of type '(?P<to>[^']+)' from an rvalue of type '(?P<from>[^']+)'$
rules.what: The function takes its parameter by reference (`int &x`), so it needs a real variable it can change - not a literal value like `5` or an expression like `a + b`.
why: Calling `f(5)` when the function is `void f(int &x)`.
fix: Pass a variable (`int v = 5; f(v);`), or change the parameter to `const int &x` / `int x` if it does not need to modify the argument.
samples: cannot bind non-const lvalue reference of type 'int&' to an rvalue of type 'int'

rules.title: C++11 feature with an old compiler setting
rules.what: Your code uses a newer C++ feature ({feature}), but the compiler is running in an old C++ standard mode.
why: Old compilers (or old IDE settings) default to C++98.
fix: Compile with `-std=c++17` (e.g. `g++ -std=c++17 prog.cpp`), or enable C++17 in your IDE's compiler settings.
samples: range-based 'for' loops only available with '-std=c++11' or '-std=gnu++11'

rules.title: Abstract class cannot be created
patterns: ^cannot declare variable '(?P<name>[^']+)' to be of abstract type '(?P<cls>[^']+)'$
rules.what: `{cls}` has a pure virtual function (`= 0`) that was not implemented, so objects of it cannot be created.
why: A derived class forgot to override every pure virtual function, or the signature differs slightly (e.g. missing const).
fix: Implement all pure virtual functions in the derived class with exactly the same signature.

example.wrong:
struct Shape { virtual double area() = 0; };
Shape s;
example.right:
struct Circle : Shape { double area() override { return 3.14; } };
Circle c;

samples: cannot declare variable 's' to be of abstract type 'Shape'

rules.title: Wrong use of a class name / constructor
patterns: ^use of class template '(?P<name>[^']+)' requires template arguments.*$
rules.what: A class or template name is used in a way C++ does not allow on line {line}.
why: A constructor written with a return type (`void Box()`).
A template such as `vector` used without its type in `< >`.
fix: Constructors have no return type; templates need their type: `vector<int> v;`.
samples: return type specification for constructor invalid
missing template arguments before 'v'

rules.title: using namespace std without any C++ header
rules.what: `using namespace std;` is written, but no C++ library header (such as `<iostream>`) is included above it, so `std` is still empty.
why: The `#include <iostream>` line is missing or comes after `using namespace std;`.
fix: Put `#include <iostream>` (and other headers you need) ABOVE `using namespace std;`.

example.wrong:
using namespace std;
int main() { cout << "hi"; }

samples: using directive refers to implicitly-defined namespace 'std'
